content: The Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) is one of the largest and oldest pediatric hospitals in the world. It has been consistently ranked as one of the top pediatric hospitals in the United States by U.S. News & World Report and Child Magazine. As of 2007, it was ranked 1 in the nation for pediatrics. The hospital is located adjacent to the University of Pennsylvania, and its physicians also serve as the pediatrics department for Penn’s School of Medicine. CHOP has over 430 beds, with 40% dedicated to neonatal, cardiac, and pediatric intensive care units. Annually, the hospital admits more than 15,000 children and handles over 600,000 visits in its emergency and outpatient departments. History In 1855, Philadelphia had a population of approximately 460,000 and recorded 10,507 deaths, with leading causes being smallpox, typhoid, and scarlet fever. During the worst month of that year, 300 children under the age of 12 died, primarily from infectious diseases. Dr. Francis West Lewis, a Philadelphia physician, was inspired by a visit to the newly established Great Ormond Street Hospital for Sick Children in London (founded in 1852). He collaborated with Dr. T.F. Penrose to establish the first children’s hospital in North America. First Hospital (1855–1866) On November 23, 1855, a small advertisement in the Philadelphia Public Ledger announced the opening of the original Children’s Hospital. It was located in a small building on Blight Street (now Watts Street) and consisted of 12 beds and a dispensary. In its first year, the hospital recorded 67 inpatient admissions and 306 outpatient visits. Second Hospital (1866–1916) After the American Civil War, the hospital relocated to 22nd Street between Locust and Walnut Streets. This facility had 35 beds and a dispensary. By 1870, surgeries were being performed at the hospital. The first resident physician was appointed in 1873. Formal medical teaching in medical and surgical clinics began in 1877. A long-term care facility, referred to as a “convalescent” branch, was opened near Overbrook. By 1892, the hospital’s capacity increased to 94 beds. In 1894, the Ingersoll Training School for nurses was established. In 1899, the convalescent facility was closed, and its program and patients were transferred to the Seashore House near Atlantic City, New Jersey. The Catherwood Milk Laboratory was established in 1900. In 1914, the first Department for the Prevention of Disease in the nation was created. Third Hospital (1916–1974) Construction of a new hospital adjacent to the second location began in 1913, and the first unit opened in 1916, extending toward 18th and Bainbridge Streets. In 1919, the hospital became affiliated with the University of Pennsylvania School of Medicine. Over the next 17 years, the affiliation grew closer, with CHOP becoming synonymous with the pediatrics department of the medical school. Most attending physicians held joint appointments at both institutions. In 1925, CHOP became affiliated with the Philadelphia Child Guidance Clinic. The first formal allocation of funds for research was recorded in 1937. The nursing school was disbanded in 1945 and converted into an affiliate training center. A six-story research building adjacent to the hospital was dedicated in 1954. In 1962, the nation’s first neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) was opened, along with a neonatal surgical unit. In 1965, the first home care program for children was established. A Clinical Research Center, under the auspices of the National Institutes of Health, was opened in 1965. Fourth Hospital (1974–Present) Construction of the current hospital complex began in 1969 on a new site on the west side of the Schuylkill River at 34th Street and Civic Center Boulevard, adjacent to the University of Pennsylvania campus. The first building opened in 1974. The current CHOP complex occupies part of the site of the old Philadelphia General Hospital and Blockley Almshouse. In 1973, a helicopter transport system for critically ill and injured children was inaugurated. CHOP celebrated its 150th anniversary on November 18, 2005. Milestones and Advances CHOP has pioneered numerous advancements in pediatric care, including the first formal medical training in pediatrics, techniques for correcting congenital heart malformations, the use of incubators for newborn intensive care, home ventilator care, and vaccine development. The hospital is undergoing a $2 billion expansion to double its size and is also constructing new research and outpatient facilities on a large site across the street on Civic Center Boulevard.
